newsitem.title: UK: Royal yacht Britannia set to be reprieved.
newsitem.headline: Royal yacht Britannia set to be reprieved.

text.p: The royal yacht Britannia is set for a reprieve from the scrapyard in a 50 million pound ($81.6 million) refit financed by private firms under a novel "timeshare" plan.

The 44-year-old yacht has steamed over one million miles in her career, playing a starring role in the handover of Hong Kong to China when she sailed out of the harbour at the end of British rule July 1.
The elegant three-masted symbol of a once mighty empire was due to be decomissioned at the end of 1997 but Britain's new Labour government is now considering other options that could save her.

Labour, victors in Britain's May 1 election, have shelved plans by the previous government to replace Britannia and may now opt for a complete refit that could give the yacht a new 20-year lease of life.

Minister without portfolio Peter Mandelson spoke of plans to "refurnish it properly so it is is good for the royal family and great for Britain too but using private finance on a lease-back arrangement."
"I hope very much that will be possible to do," he told GMTV on Sunday.
Media reports said that Queen Elizabeth and her family would pay rent to use the vessel under a "timeshare" arrangement.
Paymaster General Geoffrey Robinson will seek to persuade financiers and bankers to finance a refit and then lease the Britannia back to the government.
The ship could pay for herself after being rented out to firms for up to 70 days at a time. But the royal family would have first call on her for official functions and state visits.
The yacht is currently on a tour round the British Isles that was scheduled to be her last.
A Treasury spokesman said a number of options were now being considered that could decide the fate of the yacht used by Prince Charles for his honeymoon with Princess Diana.
Buckingham Palace declined to comment on the plans for a last-minute reprieve. "This is in the hands of the government and it is for the government to decide," a spokesman said.
Britannia's working life has virtually spanned the reign of Queen Elizabeth.
With her crew of 236 and antiquated steam plant orginally lifted from a British submarine in 1943, Britannia cost British taxpayers about eight million pounds ($13 million) a year to run.

When Conservative defence minister Michael Portillo said in January that a new $100 million yacht would be commissioned, 72 percent of Britons in a poll disapproved of government plans to pay for the yacht.
